title: Detecting Financial Fraud: A Comparative Study of Quantum-Based Supervised Learning Algorithms
journal_or_venue: Proceedings of Sixth Doctoral Symposium on Computational Intelligence (DoSCI-2025), Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
abstract_summary: This empirical study compares quantum-enhanced supervised learning approaches for financial fraud detection, evaluating four Quantum Graph Neural Network variants: VQC, QSVC, EQNN, and SQNN. The results show QSVC achieving the best balance of accuracy and precision (accuracy 91.3%, precision 92.6%, recall 86.1%, F1 89.2%), indicating its suitability for practical fraud detection while noting the need for further optimization and scalability work. This empirical study reports the demonstration of 'quantum supremacy' using a 53-qubit superconducting processor (Sycamore) to perform a speciﬁc sampling task that the authors argue would be intractable for classical supercomputers. The experiment showed the quantum device executing the task in a matter of seconds, illustrating a computational task separation between current quantum hardware and classical methods and sparking subsequent discussion on benchmarking and classical simulation optimizations. The paper presents a machine-learning framework to classify invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) from histopathology image patches using a comprehensive feature set drawn from both frequency (2D DWT, Gabor) and texture (GLCM) domains. A hybrid feature-selection pipeline reduced 268 features to 98, and experiments with KNN, decision tree, random forest, SVM and neural networks demonstrate that selection improves performance substantially—SVM and backpropagation neural network achieved the best results (around 92–93% accuracy).
methodology_description: The study implements and compares several quantum-enhanced supervised learning approaches for credit-card fraud detection using a quantum-graph-neural-network (QGNN) style pipeline. Classical preprocessing and feature-compression are applied to transaction records to reduce dimensionality and to produce concise node feature vectors. The compacted features are quantum-encoded (angle/rotation encoding) into a quantum Hilbert space and processed by parameterized variational quantum circuits (VQCs). Several QGNN variants are evaluated: Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC), Quantum Support Vector Classifier (QSVC), Estimator Quantum Neural Network (EQNN), and Sampler Quantum Neural Network (SQNN). The QGNN approach aggregates node embeddings (graph pooling/average pooling) and uses a classical linear layer on top of the quantum-processed representation for final binary class prediction (fraud / non-fraud). Models are trained and evaluated on a standard credit-card fraud dataset; performance is reported in terms of accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score, and comparisons are made across the four quantum-based methods. This paper uses a systematic literature review methodology to survey advances in quantum machine learning (QML). The authors formulated explicit research questions (e.g., state-of-the-art QML methods, applications, and practical limitations) and defined keyword-based search queries (e.g., "quantum machine learning", "quantum algorithms", "quantum neural networks"). Major academic databases and archives (for example IEEE Xplore, major peer-reviewed journals, and arXiv) were searched for publications from roughly 2015–2024. Inclusion criteria prioritized peer-reviewed studies and high-impact conference publications that present new algorithms, empirical evaluations, or clear theoretical contributions; non-refereed items and non-English sources were excluded. For each retained paper the authors extracted metadata, methodology descriptions, datasets (when present), algorithmic details, and reported empirical results. Extracted information was synthesized qualitatively to identify common trends, capabilities, hardware constraints (e.g., NISQ limitations), and open challenges. The review explicitly compared algorithmic families, use cases (e.g., quantum chemistry, optimization, secure distributed learning), and hybrid quantum–classical strategies, and it highlighted reproducibility and practical deployment issues. Limitations of the review (publication bias, rapid pace of the ﬁeld and possible omission of very recent preprints) are acknowledged. This study addresses invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) classification from histopathology image patches by extracting a comprehensive set of handcrafted features from both spatial and frequency domains, performing hybrid feature selection, and evaluating multiple classical machine-learning classifiers. Feature extraction combined frequency-based methods (2D discrete wavelet transform (DWT) decomposition into LL/LH/HL/HH subbands, and Gabor-filter bank descriptors with multiple orientations, wavelengths, phases and σ values) with texture-based descriptors (GLCM features computed at four offsets). The combined feature pool reached 268 features (220 from DWT+Gabor and 48 from GLCM). A hybrid feature-selection pipeline was applied: filter-stage selection (mutual information for frequency features and correlation-based filtering for texture descriptors) followed by a wrapper refinement using recursive feature elimination (RFE), reducing the set from 268 to 98 features (~63.3% reduction). The reduced features were used to train and evaluate KNN (k=5), Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and a Back-Propagation Neural Network (BPNN). Performance was reported with precision, recall, F-measure, accuracy and AUC-ROC, comparing results with and without feature selection to demonstrate the impact of dimensionality reduction.
algorithms_used: Gabor filter bank (multiple orientations, wavelengths, phases)
experimental_setup: The experiments used the commonly used credit card transactions dataset (creditcard.csv) as the testbed for fraud detection. Classical preprocessing and feature-compression were applied, then features were angle-encoded into quantum states and fed to variational quantum circuits. Quantum–classical hybrid training was performed using PennyLane and PyTorch-based components. Models compared: VQC, QSVC, EQNN, and SQNN. Evaluation metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score.
dataset_used: Credit card transactions dataset (commonly known as creditcard.csv) containing transactions from European cardholders (September 2013). The dataset contains 284,807 transactions with 492 labeled fraudulent transactions; all features are numeric (e.g., anonymized PCA components and Amount), and there are no missing values.

results_summary: The paper presents an empirical comparison of four quantum-inspired/quantum graph neural network algorithms for credit-card fraud detection on a highly imbalanced real-world dataset. Among the evaluated models, the Quantum Support Vector Classiﬁer (QSVC) achieved the best empirical performance (accuracy 91.3%, precision 92.6%, recall 86.1%, F1 89.2%), followed by the Variational Quantum Classiﬁer (VQC). Estimator QNN (EQNN) and Sampler QNN (SQNN) performed worse in the reported experiments. The authors conclude that QSVC offers a good balance of high precision and reasonable recall, making it a promising candidate for further optimization and potential deployment, while emphasizing the need for more work on scalability, dataset imbalance, and practical integration. The reviewed paper synthesizes recent advances in quantum machine learning (QML), highlighting both theoretical and empirical developments. Empirical milestones (e.g., Google’s 53-qubit quantum sampling experiment) demonstrate that quantum devices can outperform classical machines for narrowly deﬁned tasks. QML techniques such as QSVMs, QNNs, and variational hybrid algorithms show promise for high-dimensional pattern recognition, optimization, and quantum simulation tasks and can sometimes generalize from fewer training examples. However, substantial practical barriers persist: NISQ-era hardware limitations (qubit count, coherence, noise), data-encoding challenges, and measurement resource requirements. Pragmatic near-term strategies emphasize hybrid quantum–classical models, resource-efﬁcient measurement approaches (e.g., classical shadows), and focused application domains (quantum chemistry, optimization). Overall, QML is promising but largely conditional on future hardware and algorithmic advances. The collection of conference papers reports multiple supervised- and deep-learning based systems across medical imaging, NLP, and voice-assistant domains. Key empirical results include substantial feature-space reduction (268→98) improving invasive ductal carcinoma classifiers (notably SVM and neural networks), a MobileNetV2 CNN achieving >80% accuracy on HAM10000 dermoscopy images, a GenAI voice model achieving ~90% accuracy/relevancy vs. existing assistants, a stacked ensemble achieving ~96.4% accuracy for news classification, a Bi-LSTM+CNN producing near-perfect training accuracy with strong validation performance, a retinal vessel extraction pipeline reaching ~94.7% accuracy on DRIVE, and a HACOANN system for Twitter sentiment hitting ~93% accuracy. Authors commonly recommend expanding datasets, applying advanced feature extraction or transfer learning, and validating in more diverse/out-of-distribution scenarios.

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — Empirical evaluation (simulator-based) of four QGNN-style quantum classifiers (VQC, QSVC, EQNN, SQNN) on the standard credit-card fraud dataset shows QSVC achieving best measured metrics (Accuracy 91.3%, Precision 92.6%, Recall 86.1%, F1 89.2%).

#idea:hybrid-approach — The pipeline uses classical preprocessing (feature compression/dimensionality reduction, GraphSAGE-style neighborhood sampling) combined with angle/rotation encoding and parameterized variational circuits, showing a hybrid QPU-CPU-style workflow implemented in PennyLane + PyTorch.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Results suggest that quantum-enhanced graph / kernel approaches could be promising for fraud detection, but the paper frames these as potential directions requiring further optimization and scaling.

#limitation:simulation-only — Experiments appear to run on simulator frameworks (PennyLane) with no hardware details reported, so results do not reflect device noise, real qubit constraints, or end-to-end deployment challenges.

#limitation:data-encoding — The study relies on feature compression and angle encoding to fit data into compact quantum states, highlighting encoding/representation trade-offs needed to make the approach tractable on small simulated circuits.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Empirical demonstration (Google Sycamore, 53 qubits) of a sampling task executed orders of magnitude faster on quantum hardware than reported classical approaches, used as evidence of a computational separation.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — NISQ devices can produce meaningful empirical results for narrowly defined tasks, but short coherence times, high error rates, and limited qubit counts constrain broader applicability.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Hybrid quantum–classical models (variational circuits, VQE, QAOA) are emphasized as the pragmatic near-term path to extract benefits from noisy hardware while leveraging classical computation.
#idea:quantum-advantage — Data encoding/feature-mapping choices critically affect QML performance; representation costs may offset algorithmic gains if encoding is inefficient.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Practical techniques (adaptive gradient clipping, classical shadows, resource-efficient measurements) mitigate some NISQ limitations and improve training/stability for QML on current devices.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The claimed supremacy result spurred follow-up benchmarking and classical simulation optimizations, highlighting sensitivity of advantage claims to classical baseline improvements.

#idea:hybrid-approach — A hybrid feature-selection pipeline (filter-stage using mutual information and correlation-based filtering, followed by a wrapper RFE) reduced the feature set from 268 to 98 (~63% reduction) and consistently improved classifier performance.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Combining handcrafted frequency-domain (2D DWT, Gabor) and texture-domain (GLCM) features yields a rich 268-dimensional descriptor that, after selection, enabled strong performance from classical classifiers (notably SVM and BPNN).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Classical ML models (SVM, backpropagation NN, Random Forest) achieve high accuracies (~88–90% without selection and up to ≈90–91% metrics after selection), indicating practical applicability in the medical imaging task (but not related to quantum computing or finance).
contradictions: The paper interprets QSVC as 'suitable for practical fraud detection' based on simulator results but provides no comparison to classical baselines (e.g., classical GNNs, classical SVMs, or other ML models) — making claims of practical suitability or superiority over classical methods unsupported (contradiction:classical-vs-quantum).

The authors speculate about scaling and integration into production-grade, real-time systems while reporting only simulator-based experiments and no hardware/noise/scalability analysis; this conflicts with the claim that the approaches are ready or clearly appropriate for production deployment (contradiction:scalability).

The paper reports a clear quantum advantage (Arute et al., 2019) for a specific sampling task, but also acknowledges that classical simulation optimizations and benchmarking debates quickly narrowed the gap — indicating a contradiction between initial supremacy claims and later classical improvements (see 2019_Arute_QuantumSupremacy and subsequent classical simulation responses).

While the study demonstrates a task-specific speedup on real hardware, it simultaneously stresses NISQ hardware limitations (qubit counts, noise, coherence) that prevent straightforward scaling to practical, large-scale problems — a tension between demonstrated advantage and scalability to finance-relevant problem sizes.
